items.prompt: A binary heap already contains h elements. Report the worst-case time complexity of reading the root with peek, without modifying the heap.

feedback.reason: Peek reads the root at a known position and performs no invariant repair.

blocks.text: The heap invariant guarantees that the selected extreme is stored at the root, so the operation needs one indexed read. The number of descendants does not matter because no traversal occurs. This constant bound applies to peek only; push and pop may follow a root-to-leaf or leaf-to-root path and therefore have different costs.

constraints: `h >= 1`; empty-heap peek behavior is outside this question.

items.prompt: A binary heap contains h elements. Report the worst-case time complexity of one push or one pop that may repair the heap along one root-to-leaf path.

feedback.reason: A complete binary heap has height O(log h), and one mutation repairs at most one ancestor or descendant path.

blocks.text: Push may sift a new leaf to the root, and pop may sift a replacement root toward a leaf. Each level performs constant comparison and swap work, while the number of levels is logarithmic in the current heap size. The bound is not constant merely because the root is directly accessible, and it is not linear because unrelated branches are not scanned.

constraints: `h >= 2`, so `log h` represents a positive asymptotic height bound.

items.prompt: An algorithm processes n stream values and maintains at most k retained candidates in a binary heap. In the worst case, each value may cause one bounded heap update. Report total time and extra space.
constraints: Exclude storage for the input and final output.

feedback.reason: There are n inspections, each with at most logarithmic work in a heap whose size never exceeds k; the retained state stores at most k entries.

blocks.text: Every input value is examined once. A value may be discarded after a root comparison or may trigger push/pop repair bounded by the height of a size-k heap. The worst-case total is therefore O(n log k), with O(k) extra retained state. The bound is not O(n log n) unless the heap grows with n, and it is not O(n) in the worst case when k grows and many updates repair the heap.

items.prompt: All `n` values are already available. Compare the worst-case construction time of bottom-up binary heapify with inserting the `n` values one at a time into an initially empty heap.

feedback.reason: Bottom-up heapify has linear aggregate sift-down work, while n independent insertions can each climb logarithmic height.

blocks.text: Group internal nodes by their height `d`, the maximum number of levels they can sift toward a leaf. At most `ceil(n / 2^(d+1))` nodes have height `d`, so, up to the harmless rounding term, aggregate repair is bounded by `n · Σ(d / 2^(d+1))` for `d >= 1`. This weighted geometric sum converges to a constant, giving `O(n)` bottom-up time. Repeated insertion instead has worst-case cost `Σ O(log i)` for heap sizes `i = 1..n`, which is `O(n log n)` and is attained when many inserted keys climb near the root. The methods establish the same heap invariant, but bottom-up construction exploits the fact that most nodes have very little possible travel.

items.prompt: `k` sorted sources contain `N` values in total. A merge heap stores at most one current head per nonempty source. Report worst-case total time and extra space, excluding the output.

feedback.reason: Each of N outputs causes at most one pop and one push on a frontier bounded by k entries.

blocks.text: Every input value becomes an output exactly once. Selecting it and exposing its successor mutate a heap whose height is O(log k), so the total is O(N log k). The heap and source-position metadata use O(k) extra space. N counts iterations; k bounds per-iteration priority work. With two sources, direct merge gives O(N) time without a heap.

items.prompt: An algorithm performs n heap mutations. During the run, heap size varies but never exceeds H. What worst-case time bound follows directly from the heap-size cap?

feedback.reason: Each mutation costs at most O(log H), and there are n such mutations.

blocks.text: The precise sum depends on the size before each operation, but log hᵢ is at most log H. Summing n bounded mutation costs gives O(n log H). O(log H) omits the number of operations, while O(n) assumes H is constant or repairs never traverse height. This form transfers to bounded top-k heaps, merge frontiers, and schedulers with an explicit queue-size cap.

items.prompt: An algorithm inserts n items into an initially empty binary heap and then removes all n items. What worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds should be reported?

feedback.reason: There are 2n logarithmic worst-case mutations, and the heap may hold all n items between phases.

blocks.text: Each push and pop can traverse heap height O(log n), so n insertions plus n removals give O(n log n) worst-case time. The backing array stores up to n entries, giving O(n) auxiliary space. A bottom-up heapify could reduce construction cost, but the repeated removals still contribute O(n log n).

constraints: The heap is materialized in memory and no output storage is counted.

items.prompt: A streaming top-k algorithm processes n values with a heap that never exceeds k retained entries. Each value may cause one push and one pop. What time and auxiliary-space bounds follow?

feedback.reason: The priority work depends on the retained frontier size k, not on the full stream length n.

blocks.text: Each arrival performs constant checks and at most logarithmic heap repairs at size k. Across n arrivals this is O(n log k), with O(k) retained entries. A scan of all history per arrival would be larger; calling the time O(n) would hide nonconstant heap repair unless k is explicitly constant.

constraints: 1 <= k <= n and the heap stores only the retained frontier.

items.prompt: A lazy-deletion priority queue performs n insertions and n logical deletions; each physical stale entry is purged at most once when it reaches the root. What amortized time bound follows?

feedback.reason: Every inserted entry is pushed once and physically popped at most once, with logarithmic repair per heap mutation.

blocks.text: Lazy deletion changes when removal occurs, not the total number of physical heap operations: at most O(n) pushes and O(n) stale or active pops. With heap size O(n), each costs O(log n), giving O(n log n) amortized time. Until purged, stale entries can occupy O(n) memory, so logical deletion does not imply constant space.

constraints: No periodic compaction reduces the physical heap below the inserted-entry bound.

items.prompt: A client performs n heap insertions, n peek operations, and n removals. Which cost distinction should the complexity answer make?

options.text: Peek is O(1) per operation, while push and pop are O(log h) in a heap of size h; the total is dominated by the mutations.
Every operation is O(log h) because reading the root requires descending the heap.
All operations are O(1) because the root is always stored at index zero.
Peek is O(h) because all entries must be checked to validate the root.

feedback.reason: Root access is constant-time; only mutations may traverse a repair path.

blocks.text: A valid heap invariant guarantees the root is the required extreme, so peek reads one array position in O(1). Push and pop can move an element up or down height O(log h). For n operations of each kind, the O(n log h) mutation work dominates the O(n) peeks.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_constant: Mutation can move an element through the heap height even though root access is constant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.peek_linear: The heap invariant already summarizes the extreme at the root.

constraints: The heap invariant is maintained after every mutation.

items.prompt: What is the asymptotic cost of building a heap from an array of n values using bottom-up heapify?
constraints: All n values are initially available.
The heap is built in place or with linear auxiliary storage.

options.text: Bottom-up heapify is O(n) because most nodes are near leaves and move only a small distance.
options.explanation: The sum of subtree heights is linear.

options.text: It must be O(n log n) because inserting n values one at a time is the only heap construction method.
options.explanation: Repeated insertion has that cost, bottom-up heapify is different.

options.text: It is O(1) because only the root needs correction.
options.explanation: Every internal node may need a sift-down.

options.text: Each internal node scans the whole array, making construction quadratic.
options.explanation: Sift-down follows its own subtree height, not the entire array.

feedback.reason: Heap construction cost depends on the construction method.

blocks.text: Bottom-up heapify starts at the last internal nodes and sifts down. Although an individual node can move logarithmically, the many shallow nodes make the total linear; repeated push is O(n log n).

k is smaller than or equal to n.

options.text: At most O(n log k) time and O(k) auxiliary space, with a constant-time rejection or O(log k) replacement path.
options.explanation: The heap is bounded while every stream item may be examined.

options.text: The method is O(n log n) time and O(n) space because all stream values remain in the heap.
options.explanation: A bounded top-k heap discards most values.

options.text: Both time and space are O(1) because k is treated as a constant in all contracts.

blocks.text: The scan costs at least O(n) to read the stream. Each item can trigger an O(log k) replacement, and the heap stores k entries; if k is a fixed constant this simplifies but should not hide the parameter.
